description: We are HopeMaxxxing, a team of developers, designers, and problem solvers dedicated to building high-impact solutions for tomorrow. By combining rapid prototyping, clean architecture, and a relentless focus on real-world utility, we turn ambitious concepts into functional software. We believe that technology should serve as a force multiplier for positive change, and we are here to build the next generation of tools that empower communities and optimize for a better future.
summary:
When people pick a place on Earth to rehearse Moon or Mars missions, they mostly go by how it looks. We wanted to check with numbers instead, and we picked our own country. Kazakhstan is where Soyuz crews land, NASA astronauts included, but almost nobody has studied it as an analog.

We ran the same code on four groups: real landing sites on the Moon and Mars, 16 places in Kazakhstan, 10 famous analog sites, and about 200 random desert points. If a Kazakh site couldn't beat a random desert, we didn't count it.

Some things held up. The Soyuz landing zone is much flatter than the steppe around it. The ground temperature swings 72 K between summer and winter. Shunak crater still has about a quarter of its original depth.

Some things didn't: overall terrain shape and radar roughness are no better than random desert, and we say so. The code is open and works on any region.
details:
What it does and how it works

Steppe to Mars tests whether places in Kazakhstan can stand in for the Moon or Mars. We looked at 16 sites, including the steppe where Soyuz capsules land. To avoid fooling ourselves, every measurement was run with the same code on four groups: real Moon and Mars landing sites, our Kazakh sites, 10 well-known analogs like Meteor Crater and White Sands, and about 200 random desert points. A Kazakh site only counts if it does better than the random points. We measured slope at three scales, temperature swings, how bright the ground is, crater depth, salt, radar roughness and distance to the nearest airport. There is no single score. Each property is shown on its own, with a line saying where the comparison stops working.

What we found

- The Soyuz landing zone is very flat: 0.12° against 0.29° for random steppe. NASA's ICESat-2 laser data shows the same at a finer scale.

- The ground swings 72 K between the hottest and coldest month. Random deserts swing 54 K.

- The steppe is about as bright as Mars landing sites.

- Shunak crater has kept about a quarter of the depth a fresh crater would have.

- The salt flat of Lake Inder and the dry Aral seabed look saltier than every random point.

- What didn't work: overall terrain shape, radar roughness, ground patterns and thermal inertia don't make Kazakhstan special. We left these in on purpose.

Benefits and intended impact

Crews already land in this steppe and get picked up there, so it is a real place to practise mapping a landing zone, recovering a crew and testing equipment in heat and cold. It also puts a region on the analog map that researchers have mostly skipped. The code is open, so anyone can run the same test on their own country.

Tools

Python (numpy, scipy, rasterio, matplotlib), Leaflet and Chart.js for the map and charts, GitHub and Vercel for hosting. Data from NASA (NASADEM, ICESat-2, MODIS, LRO LOLA and Diviner, MGS MOLA and TES), ESA (Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2), JAXA (ALOS) and CSA (RADARSAT-1). No hardware. We used Claude (AI) to help write code and text. Every number comes from running the code on the data we list.

How it is creative

Most projects pick a site and argue for it. We tried to prove ours wrong first. Before each test we wrote down what result would count against us, and we published the failures next to the successes.

Factors we considered

Earth can't copy the gravity, air or radiation of the Moon and Mars, so we never claim a full match. The daily temperature swing here is about 30 K, far less than on Mars, and it snows in winter. We only used satellite data, so soil strength and rocks are unknown. We also checked whether our elevation data could be trusted on flat ground, and used a second data set where it couldn't.
